subject: Stan/PyStan example from Economics/Finance/Investment: Investing in hydropower upgrades.

messages.author: 608e75a8d4303862
messages.subject: Stan/PyStan example from Economics/Finance/Investment: Investing in hydropower upgrades.
parts:
Hi everyone, 

First, a big thanks too the Stan development team for putting out an amazing (group of) tools. I've been learning and working with Stan for about a year now, and am more and more amazed by what it can do and how helpful and user-oriented the development team is. 

I thought I would try to contribute in however small way by posting the Stan code and data for a project I am currently working on. But a strong warning: I am a Stan amateur, and while the code runs and Stan converges (quickly), I make no claims to my code being written in an optimum way or the statistics being particularily well thought out (yet). But for a complete beginner, perhaps it will still be instructive. On the flip side, should anyone see obvious problems with my code or statistics, I would be happy to hear criticisms. 

Let me start by trying to explain what I am doing. The research topic is to try to analyse the investment decision of hydropower plant owners who decide to upgrade their plants by installing new generators or upgrading existing generators. The dependent variable is then a 0/1 variable of whether or not an investment happens in a given year (2012-2014) for a particular plant. In particular, the question we want to pursue is what relation this investment decision has to the amount of renewable wind/solar energy that already exist in the area and how this interacts with a policy variable, which is whether there exists a Renewable Portfolio Standards that requires a certain percentage of renewables in the energy mix in the state where a hydroplant exists. 

I guess you have to decide yourself if this is interesting, but the idea in my mind is that the relationship could go either way. Hydropower - especially with a reservoir - can do a good job of balancing out the intermittency of solar or wind - that is the fact that you can not control when it is sunny or when it is windy. So a lot of solar and wind could lead to increased investment in hydropower plants. On the other hand, if owners are just trying to fill a quota - of which hydro counts, then we could expect a substitute effect where new hydro is installed instead of solar/wind. 

a data file in "pickle" format is included with this post. Below I will copy the Stan code and the very short PyStan call. 

In the stan code below, I will have 4 levels in the model hierarchy: observation level which is a plant-year. Each plant-year is then grouped by plant (so every plant has three observations - 2012, 2013, 2014). In turn each plant belongs to a certain Transmission System Owner (TSO) - the entity that owns the power lines connecting the different power plants and the rest of the grid. We can expect a lot of variation here - some TSOs are vertically integrated utilities that also own the plants, other times power plant owners are seperate and private. Finally, I group the TSOs into two groups - those that operate in states with renewable portfolio standards and those that don't.

Starting at the model section of the stan code, I model the investment decision as a bernoulli model with logit link function. Going up a level to the transformed parameter section, the fitted values, y_hat are modelled as a random effect for each plant b_obs, a random effect for the report year, bry, and an error term epsilon, which is meant to capture over dispersion - that is an excess of zeros over what would be expected. 

Going up a level in the transformed parameters sections, I model each plant-level random effect b_obs as an additive function of an intercept plus the effects of 5 plant-level variables: whether the plant has a reservoir, whether it uses pumped storage (can pump up water to a higher level at low demand times, in order to generate electricity at high demand) whether the power plant is a vertically integrated utility or an Independent Power Producer, the nameplate capacity of the plant and the year the plant started operation. 

Again, moving up in the transformed parameters section, The coefficients on the plant level variables are modelled as an additive function of a coefficient on the percent of intermittents, mu_b of (wind and solar) in a TSO and a random effect. The mu_b variables are in turn modeled as having seperate distributions between RPS and non-RPS states. The posterior distributions of the mu_b coefficients are then what I am most interested in - comparing those in RPS and non-RPS states. 

Stan Code: 

data{
int<lower = 0> N; // number of observations
int<lower = 0> Y; //number or reporting years 2012-2014
int<lower = 0> R; //RPS Transmission system owner (does TSO operate in at least one RPS state)
int<lower = 0> S; //TSOs in data set
int<lower = 0> P; //Number of individual power plants
int<lower = 0> K; //number of plant-level co-variates

int<lower = 1, upper=3> report_year[N]; //normalized 2012-2014 to 1-3
int<lower=0, upper=1432> plant[N]; indicator of which plant is in each observation
int<lower=0, upper=1> investment[N]; //no/yes investment made on plant

vector[P] op_year; //first year of operation
vector[P] nameplate; //nameplate capacity of plant
vector[P] utility; //is utility (1) or IPP (0)
vector[P] pumped_storage; //is pumped storage (1) or not(0)
vector[P] isrsrvr; //is reservoir
int<lower=1, upper=234> TSO[P]; //TSO indicator of plant
         vector[S] perc_intermittent;
int<lower=1, upper=2> isRPS[S]; //indicator of whether TSO operates in RPS state 1= not RPS, 2= RPS
}

transformed data{
real mean_nameplate;
real<lower=0> sd_nameplate;
vector[P] st_nameplate;
real<lower=0, upper=1> mean_perc_intermittent;
real<lower=0> sd_perc_intermittent;
vector[S] st_perc_intermittent;

mean_nameplate <- mean(nameplate);
sd_nameplate <- sd(nameplate);
st_nameplate <- (nameplate-mean_nameplate)/(2*sd_nameplate);

mean_perc_intermittent <- mean(perc_intermittent);
sd_perc_intermittent <- sd(perc_intermittent);
st_perc_intermittent <- (perc_intermittent-mean_perc_intermittent)/(2*sd_perc_intermittent);
}

parameters{
real bry[Y]; //random effect for report 
real epsilon; //extra error term for overdispersion
real<lower=0> sigma_epsilon; //sd of overdispersion param.
real<lower=0> sigma_bry; //sd of year effects
matrix[K, R] mu_b; //average for 5 plant level explanatory coefficients
matrix[K, S] re_b; //random effect for each coeff
}


transformed parameters {
real y_hat[N];
real b_obs[P];
matrix[K, S] b_p; // matrix of coefficients

for (s in 1:S){
for (k in 1:K){
b_p[k, s] <- mu_b[k, isRPS[s]]*st_perc_intermittent[s]
+ re_b[k,s];
}
}

for (p in 1:P){
b_obs[p]<- b_p[1, TSO[p]] +
b_p[2, TSO[p]]*pumped_storage[p] + 
b_p[3, TSO[p]]*isrsrvr[p] +
b_p[4, TSO[p]]*utility[p] + 
b_p[5, TSO[p]]*st_nameplate[p];
}

for (i in 1:N){
y_hat[i] <- b_obs[plant[i]] + bry[report_year[i]] + epsilon;
}
}

model{
bry ~ cauchy(0, sigma_bry); //vectorized, Y
for (k in 1:K){
mu_b[k] ~ cauchy(0, 2.5); //vectorized, R
  re_b[k] ~ cauchy(0, 2.5); //vectorized, S 
}
investment ~ bernoulli_logit(y_hat); //vectorized, n
epsilon ~ normal(0, sigma_epsilon); //overdispersion parameter
}


PyStan call:
import pystan
import pickle

pp_stan_data = pickle.load(open("pp_stan_data3.pkl", 'rb'))
pp_fit3 = pystan.stan(file="/Users/johannesmauritzen/research/power_plants/pp_stan3.stan",
data = pp_stan_data, iter=1000, chains=4)


#In addition, we can chart the histograms of the mu_b posterios:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

pp_extr = pp_fit3.extract(permuted=True) 
mu_b = pp_extr["mu_b"]

pvars = ["intercept", "pumped_storage", "isrsrvr", "utility", "st_nameplate"]
rps_vars = ["not_rps", "rps"]
df_mu_b = pd.DataFrame()
for i, p in enumerate(pvars):
for j, r in enumerate(rps_vars):
df_var = p+"_" + r
df_mu_b[df_var] = pd.Series(mu_b[:, i, j])

#chart the histograms
plt.figure
df_mu_b.hist(bins=50, normed=True, layout=(5,2), figsize=(10,15))
plt.show()

Thanks. And good timing. The good folks at QuantEcon were
just asking for PyStan examples in econometrics if you're
interested in putting the example into Jupyter and contributing
it:

http://quantecon.org/notebooks.html

I suggested they make it clear that authors would maintain
copyright and I think they're going to do that.

The only thing I'd suggest for the code is vectorizing
the Cauchy sampling statements --- you don't need the loop.

to_vector(mu_b) ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
to_vector(re_b) ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

And I'd describe epsilon as an intercept in the GLM and use
a different letter for it.

You might also want priors on all your parameters --- I
don't see any on sigma_bry, for instance.

- Bob
